questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+16} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{[{x}^{2}-1]^{′}}{[x+16]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{2x}{1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-x-1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{e}^{x}-x-1]^{′}}{[\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-x-1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1} & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{e}^{x}-1]^{′}}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to 0}{e}^{2/{x}^{2}}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2/{x}^{2}}}{(\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{e}^{2/{x}^{2}}]}^{′}}{{[\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2/{x}^{2}}(-\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4{e}^{2/{x}^{2}}\cancel{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}}{\cancel{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}} \\  & =4{lim}_{x\to 0}{e}^{2/{x}^{2}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{4}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{ln\,(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[ln\,(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)]}^{′}}{[1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{ln\,(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}^{′}}{{[(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)]}^{′}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$
